speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext: The first shipment left last week.

When this item was up for discussion some time ago I registered an objection against the practice followed by the department of going to the stockyards to buy brood sows rather than obtaining them from breeders of pure bred swine. Will the minister give the committee the details of what has been done during the past year along this line. How many sows have been purchased in this way for distribution among the farmers for use as breeding animals?
I am informed by the deputy that he has not that information for the past year.

I think it is a very unwise policy to purchase animals in this way for distribution among farmers, particularly when there are so many live stock breeders who are doing such good work in breeding pure bred animals. They are helping, at considerable expense to themselves, to build up the breeding stock of this country, but if these animals are purchased at the stockyards the breeders will have no encouragement whatever to continue the work they are doing. They have rendered a wonderful service to the dominion by the production of pure bred hogs, cattle and other animals. Rather than continue in this way, I think it would be better if the department discontinued this service entirely and let the farmers buy from the breeders or wherever else they wish. It would be unfair to the pure bred live stock breeders to continue this practice any longer.

I can understand that there may be some objection to this policy, but there are also some advantages. I have shipped at one time as many as thirty or forty pure bred Yorkshire hogs to market, and many other producers have done the same thing. By there being some one at the market to make selections, many of those animals are saved from slaughter. Quite often the community in which the animals are bred is not such that they can be disposed of to advantage. Many farmers who would like to take advantage of such a distribution do not live in the immediate vicinity. We are trying to work out a policy whereby these animals will be selected at the local points rather than at the stockyards. That would provide some improvement over the present system. The department will be more than pleased to cooperate with the breeders in providing a more convenient distribution of pure bred sires.

The minister's answer goes a long way to prove just what I have said. These pure bred live stock breeders are forced to send their animals to market because they have no other market for them. They will never have a market so long as these animals are distributed in the way they are at present. I think the proper thing to do would be to purchase the animals from the pure bred live stock breeders. I believe these animals could be got for a very small premium over the prevailing market price for slaughter animals. That would assist the breeders and encourage them in the work they are doing.

I agree with what the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) has said. I do not think the department is giving the pure bred live stock breeders of this country sufficient assistance. About the only market they have is the ordinary meat auction, as one might call it. Considerable advancement has been made with reference to advanced registration of pure bred swine, and serious consideration has been given to initiating a record of performance in connection with swine, such as we have with dairy cattle. It seems to me

Supply-Agriculture-Production
that the department is giving the pure bred live stock breeder very little incentive to carry on a work which is essential to the production of high-class bacon. Has any consideration been given to the payment of 'bonuses for the production of pure bred swine, such as are paid in connection with cattle and sheep?

The bonus policy in connection with swine has been largely done away with. This policy was in force generally some years ago, but it is not now in operation in a number of provinces. The service in connection with registration and all that goes with it is given to the breeders of pure bred swine as well as to the breeders of other pure bred live stock. However, the situation in connection with hogs is a little different from that prevailing in connection with cattle or horses. The price of a pure bred sire, as far as cattle or horses are concerned, is much higher than the price of a pure bred hog. The same thing is true with regard to females. For example, when you ship hogs to market, even if they are pure bred, you would get in the west probably fifteen or sixteen dollars a head for them. It is very difficult to make selections on the farm pay the cost of those selections and add that cost on to the price of the animal. But when the individual can go perhaps to the local yard from which the hog is shipped or to the stock yard to which it is shipped, he can purchase pretty much at the market price. In addition, the amount of money involved in the animal itself renders it difficult to add the cost of the service on to it, which would mean going around and selecting the hogs where they are to be found on the farm. That is one thing which it is difficult to overcome, the matter of cost alone. When you are dealing with a bull or a stallion, it is an entirely different matter. There you can make selections and add on the cost of selection, the cost of inspection, and all that kind of thing without doubling the price of the animal, but with the hog you would probably more than double the price. I would say this, that I think the results which have been obtained across Canada from one end to the other in the improvement of swine is a fair indication that the services of the department have been not only appreciated but effective.

Perhaps the minister did not get my point. I believe the department would be well advised to give consideration to the encouragement of the production of high-class, pure bred swine that come up to the standard required and have the record of performance credentials. I see

no more serious difficulty in providing a system of general application with regard to hogs than in providing one with regard to sheep. I quite agree with the minister that great strides have been made in assisting in the production of better swine throughout the country, because farmers take advantage of the pure bred swine that are placed on the market; but that is more or less drying up the fountain from which the better swine have come; and while it slightly improves the general quality and general standard throughout the country, it does not offer much incentive to the breeders to whom the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) has referred.
As to advanced registry, I observe in last year's report that the department was completing arrangements for two advanced registry test stations, one in Edmonton and one in Saskatoon, and I should like to know what progress has been made in that regard and whether the department has given consideration to the establishment of advanced registry test stations at other points throughout the dominion. If we are going to keep in step with the improvement made in other countries in quality of production, special efforts should be made and special encouragement given by the department to the swine breeders throughout this country, so that breeding swine with special credentials as to record of performance might be more widely distributed. The department might well seriously consider the taking of special steps for the encouragement of pure bred swine because, after all, the swine from which we produce our better bacon to-day are all pure bred or eligible for registration. I quite agree that the small price secured for pure bred swine does deprive breeders from having a record of their breeding in many instances; but recently great strides have been taken with respect to advanced registry tests and records of performance credentials, and that is fundamental if we are steadily to improve the quality of our swine. But I am speaking more with reference to the encouragement of the breeder of recorded pure bred swine, than of what might be called the commercial breeder, who is merely taking advantage of the better hog he gets at the ordinary market price.

We already have a premium
on first-class hogs and I think that might perhaps serve the purpose. It is extremely important that our bacon should be properly displayed in the old country. For many years we have heard that we have never had a proper display of our bacon in the old land. We have also heard that our Canadian packing organizations do not wish to have a proper

Supply-Agriculture-Production
display of our bacon in the old land because they say that if the price of our export bacon, which comprises 15 per cent of our production, goes up then the price of the 85 per cent we consume at home would also go up, and if the price of the 85 per cent for home consumption goes up, it will come in competition with fowl, fish, eggs and salmon, and we shall not have the turnover in bacon that we now have. Their interest is in looking after the packer. Our interest is to see that we get the highest possible price for our Canadian bacon.
I have received a number of letters complaining of our Canadian display, and I have one here which I got from Glasgow only two days ago, from a drover of my home village. He visited the empire exhibition in Glasgow and viewed the situation in regard to our export cattle and hogs. I will read a few sentences from his letter:
I came to Glasgow on a cattle boat from Montreal for three reasons: first, I wanted to see how Canadian cattle were being handled for export; second, I wanted to see what Canada in particular had to show in the empire show windows at the empire exhibition; and third, I just wanted to see what sort of country our Canadian pioneers came from.
X have been greatly impressed by the beauty and historical interest of Scotland. I have just finished going through Edinburgh castle and I am writing this as I did the enclosure, in the waiting room in the castle. Canada had the most pretentious building on Dominion avenue at the exhibition, but I don't think it would sell Canada to the British Isles. While Australia had a more modest building, I believe her display was much more businesslike.
Peter C. McTavish.
That letter, as I said, was from Glasgow, from the empire exhibition.

If I might make the
suggestion, the remarks just made by my hon. friend relate to item No. 4S5. We are now on the item for the production of live stock and poultry, and I would rather reserve until we reach the other item, any remarks I have to make in reply to my hon. friend.
To deal with the questions raised by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), the first of these advanced registry establishments that was built was in Ontario. Later there was one placed in Quebec, and later another in Prince Edward Island, and one in Nova Scotia, which serves both Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Last year again there was one built in Saskatoon, as my hon. friend indicated, and one in Edmonton. This year we are rebuilding the one in Ontario; that is, we are building a more up-to-date plant.
Where?

Near Waterloo, in the same vicinity where the old one was established. That is now being arranged for. The desire is to promote the production of the best strain of Yorkshire hogs, particularly, right across Canada, and to encourage breeders in producing them by giving them this registry and also a test of the production under certain feeding regulations. That is being done at all these plants, and the work will be enlarged as funds are available.
No consideration has been given to the breeders who produce the desired type of hogs for breeding purposes?

Of course the present system contemplates that they will reap a premium on the sales when their live stock is sold. I think it has been the experience that they do, as a result of the records given by and maintained by the government.

When this item was before the committee on a former occasion, I think it was May 25, I tried to persuade the minister to give consideration to the live stock breeders of Saskatchewan by way of providing sires. I wonder if he can tell us what he proposes to do to assist Saskatchewan live stock breeders this summer, and if he has reconsidered his ideas? At that time he was not very favourably disposed.

We have not the figures made up yet for this year. The work is now being carried on. But I gave the figures, I believe, on two previous occasions, when we were on the general estimates and also on the date mentioned. The number of bulls put out in Saskatchewan was, last year, 65, and the previous year, 70; in Manitoba 61 last year and 52 the previous year; in Alberta last year 78 and the previous year 88. In addition to this policy of putting out bulls in the communities, we are this year in Saskatchewan putting bulls into the community pastures that were established. This year 18 are being placed in those pastures, to be used by those adjacent to them.
How many of those pastures are in Saskatchewan?
All eighteen are in Saskatchewan.
Can the minister give us any idea as to the number of breeding stock, females, in the pastures?

If it would serve just as well, I should prefer to deal with these figures

when we are discussing rehabilitation. I shall then have the figures available of the number of cattle served in each of the pastures.
How many sires is the department putting out this year in Saskatchewan under the loaning scheme?

The number has not yet been fully determined. As I have just indicated, we are now supplying the pastures and other areas. I am not able to give the completed figure for this year. It will be a number greater than last year.

There is just one suggestion I wish to offer to the minister. Thinking over our live stock industry and the condition it is in at the present time, and realizing that we are not making very much headway in developing a better quality of beef cattle-I am speaking particularly of beef cattle at the present time-I have come to the conclusion that the production of good live stock should be left entirely with the provinces, each of which has a department of agriculture. Over this large dominion, far-flung as it is, the federal government cannot undertake to supervise better sires for our live stock; therefore, I believe, it should be left entirely to the provinces. But I think the federal department could assist in the marketing of our products; I would say that that is their job. I believe also that they should supply funds whereby the provinces could give bonuses in the production of better sires. I wish just to throw out that suggestion. I know that in the past the different provinces have had policies of their own, sometimes overlapping with the policies of the federal government. But I am firmly convinced that the production end should be left to the province, with the federal department assisting in every way possible in providing a market and also giving financial aid. When I read of the action which has been

taken, in particular, by Ireland, which is our greatest competitor in the old country market -the policies that country has adopted, the strides it has made in producing better feeder cattle for the British market-I am amazed that we in Canada have just leaned on our oars and have not made use of the advantages which we enjoy. It is all right to send Stocker and feeder cattle to Great Britain, but we should send what the market demands. We are not doing so in any quantities. Most of our feeder cattle, store cattle that go to the old country markets, are the progeny of dairy and dual purpose bulls. Can you expect them to compete successfully with Ireland, which is using the very best beef bulls it can buy in Scotland and in England? We in Canada should be concerned in providing the very best type of beef bulls we can secure, not limiting them to any one beef breed, but getting the best we can in all breeds, thereby giving the market what it demands. The same thing applies exactly to the United States. Those two countries provide us with our markets, and if we have not the initiative and the ambition to provide ourselves with the very best stock we can possibly obtain to supply those markets, then I say there is something seriously wrong.

I wish to take this opportunity particularly to thank the Minister of Agriculture for making this grant:	Our Discovery Day celebration, the day on which we celebrate the discovery of gold in the Yukon, is on August 17, and fairs are held in the capital city, Dawson, and at White Horse and Mayo. At White Horse, Dawson and Mayo, tourist steamers call and tourists are interested in seeing what our country will produce. In the three months of the growing season when we have practically twenty-four hours of daylight or sunlight, the country produces almost all the vegetables that one gets on the outside, and our flowers are unusually beautiful. Some of our gardens rival in beauty those of the "outside" world, as we call it. Prizes are offered for the best display of flowers and the best display of vegetables. There is now one experimental farm in the vicinity of Carmacks. I do not believe that any grant is given to that farm, but seeds and roots are sent to Mr. Brown and he in turn, I believe, sends samples of the foodstuffs he has raised in that part of the world. Yukoners, I am sure, will be particularly pleased, because while this amount is not large it will at least show them that the government is taking an interest in the agricultural work away in the north country.

I am not approaching this in a critical spirit at all, but I should like ta point out that the original idea of the Cold Storage Act-I think that is the act under which subsidies are granted-was that it would be a service to producers; that was the foundation of it. It was with that thought in mind that parliament passed the act, and it has been carried on ever since. Now the strange thing is that over a long period of years since this act first came into operation there has grown up a tendency on the part of those who control some of the cold storage plants to use the plant as a method of enhancing their own profits rather than stabilizing the market for the producers. I do not apply this to all. A substantial number of those named by the minister are cooperatives, and they are not included in this at all. I am referring to the cold storage plants located in certain of our cities. I believe the department should make a careful study of these to ascertain whether the large contributions, running into many millions of dollars, that have been made out of the public treasury, are being used for the enhancement of private companies rather than to stabilize the market. I did not know that this item was coming up to-day, or I would have been fortified with more data.
Let me give one illustration. For the last ten years statistics have been published from time to time with regard to the amount of butter in storage. I looked at these the other day and I believe there is something like 20,000,000 pounds of butter now in storage. Hon. members who are familiar with this business will understand my illustration. The flush period of production in Canada is from June to September, tapering off, of course, as the grass dries up in the latter months of the summer. As we pass into the winter, when the cattle have to go under shelter, the production drops off. Usually the cold storage accumulation around September is in the neighbourhood of 20,000,000 pounds, and this will gradually diminish from about the end of October. Frequently the substantial portion of this accumulation has disappeared by February or March.
When the increase in storage ceases around the month of September the price paid to the farmer for butter fat ought to increase and continue to increase until the middle of the winter. Frequently the farmer does not get the advantage of increased butter fat prices until January, February or March. Mark you, the natural conditions are fairly steady. The large corporations, such as the Eastern Dairies, argue that an increased price should

not be paid because of the presence of this accumulation still in storage. This happens as regularly as the seasons. My conviction is that the large dairy companies have used their storage facilities for their own profit rather than to assist the farmer.
Let me put the story the other way around. When this legislation was approved parliament realized that Canada was unique, as compared with New Zealand and certain other countries, in that we had a very cold winter season but a summer season of prolific production. Parliament accepted the view that subsidies should be paid to provide cold storage facilities in order that fair prices might be maintained and that the farmer might receive a higher price for his butter fat during the winter. It was felt that the production could be sold at a price which would enable the cold storage company to pay the farmer a fair price in the summer. But that is not the way it has worked out. To use the words the head of one of these corporations uttered some time ago, "There is the consumer dollar from which must be obtained the cost of freight, the cost of processing and our profit, and the farmer gets what is left."
That is an absolutely false philosophy; yet it dominates the butter business, and also the cheese business to a certain extent. The same philosophy dominates the hog and bacon market. I implore the minister to give some thought to this philosophy that works eternally against the farmer. My contention is that there should be a fair price paid to the farmer. That should be your kicking-off point. Then you have the cost of processing, cold storage, freight, handling and distribution. The function of parliament should be to watch these intervening processes and see that they do not become too costly. Naturally I am just as much interested in protecting the consumer as I am in seeing that the farmer gets a fair deal. Parliament should exercise its discretion and control as far as possible.
I venture to say that scores of millions of dollars have been contributed to assist in providing these cold storage facilities. I recall one instance where a grant of a couple of million dollars was made. These cold storage companies that have received millions of dollars from the public treasury ought not to be allowed to use these facilities to control the market for their own advantage. These facilities should be used for the stabilizing of the market so that the farmer may receive a fair price for his butter fat and other products involved in the cold storage business.

I want to discuss the question of the handling of live stock in the public stockyards. The public stockyards were undoubtedly established for the purpose of providing an impartial and, shall I say, government supervised market to which the producer could send his live stock and be assured of competitive buying. If anything intervenes that destroys the competitive nature of the business at the buying end, obviously the shipper or producer of live stock will suffer. I am convinced, from considerable study tliat I have given to this matter, that in our live stock markets, particularly Winnipeg and Toronto, which are the two main ones-and I would add Edmonton to a certain extent; as to Montreal I would hesitate to say very much, because I am impressed with the competitive nature of that market-there has grown up over the years an element of control which deprives the farmer of his right as an individual producer to a fair marketing system. One very important factor is the competition of direct trucking to the abattoirs, but I am not going to discuss that question to-day. The effect of it is that the large packing industries are able by direct shipments to maintain such a backlog of supply that they are able temporarily, if they wish, almost to ignore the public market. That [DOT]is the condition to which that form of competition with the public market has grown. But what I am going to deal with now are the abuses which I believe are prevalent in the market itself.
The public market, or stockyard, is served by commission houses or brokers who handle the stock on a commission basis for the producer, acting as a medium between him and the buyer. The buyers consist in the main of the large packing companies; but in addition there are what are known as the wholesalers who purchase some portion of their supplies from private abattoirs, separate from the packing companies. These wholesalers are a distinctly healthy element in the buyers market, looking at it from the standpoint of the farmer. They constitute something in the nature of a check on the overwhelming power of the large packing concerns. I have
before me a very definite case which the minister will recall I brought to his attention. I wish to present this case to the committee as an illustration of what goes on.
It will be noted as I read the correspondence that the minister on the advice of his officials is under the impression that the practices with which I shall deal are not prevalent on the market. This is the issue I take with the Department of Agriculture. It is extremely difficult to discuss a matter of this kind without appearing to be critical of the minister. I shall certainly be critical of him as far as it is deserved, but that is not my point. My point is that here is a grievance, of which this case that I shall cite is only a type. It exists; it is prevalent; I know it is prevalent: all I am asking is that the matter shall be grappled with and the practices stopped.
On March 11 last I brought to the attention of the minister a case where some 800 lambs were brought to the Toronto market. They were offered for sale, and the Toronto municipal abattoir, a responsible organization, bid on 200 of these lambs. The representative of Canada Packers, Limited, indicated to the commission house that if they sold a part of this lot to anyone else he, the buyer for Canada Packers, would not bid for or take the balance. And when it is understood, as it must be to understand this question at all, that Canada Packers exercise an overwhelming influence on our markets, particularly the stockyards, by virtue of the large quantities that they buy, it will be clear that any commission man who goes in the face of or does anything contrary to the desires of Canada Packers is subject to be blacklisted and driven out of business, as some of them have been driven out of business by that organization. In this instance the Canada Packers buyer declared that he would not buy the balance if the commission house dared to sell the 200 lambs to the Toronto municipal abattoir. The commission man told -the municipal abattoir that he was sorry, and turned the lot over to Canada Packers. The municipal abattoir was short of lambs for its trade. That abattoir supplies the wholesalers. Fortunately, by scurrying around, he managed to get part of his supply. But the day after,-the letter will show this-the sales agent of Canada Packers rang him up and offered to sell him carcases. The point is this: Canada Packers did not require for their own requirements the 800 lambs; they could easily have spared the 200; but they said, No, all or none. The point is that when they offered to sell to the municipal abattoir a supply of carcases they quoted a price half

I have had the complaint checked. The report is that what actually occurred was as follows. On March 7th, Dunn and Levack sold 800 western lambs to Canada Packers at $9.25. It will be noted that this letter makes reference to the fact that I did not disclose the name of the person. Well, I did not have the authority to do so at the time, but I did secure it and I then furnished the minister with the original letter from the municipal abattoir, which I shall now read. This is dated March 9, 1938, and is addressed to me:
Having knowledge of your attitude toward mass buying and unethical business practices, we beg to take this opportunity of drawing your attention to the "cut-throat" tactics adopted by the Canada Packers Limited on the Union stockyards this week in regard to the purchase of live lambs.
On Monday of this week there were 800 western lambs for sale by the commission firm of Dunn and Levack.
One buyer was instructed to purchase 200 lambs (one car load).
The commission people were perfectly willing to sell us 200 lambs "out" of the 800 lot, but

they were told by the Canada Packers' buyer (Mr. It. McDonald) that of the 800 lot were broken they would not take the balance. Mr. McDonald was instructed by head office that it was a case of "all or nothing."
The commission house had no other alternative but to sell the entire 800 lambs to Canada Packers Limited.
This, of course, left us without a lamb in our coolers and to add insult to injury a Canada Packers' salesman called us by telephone Tuesday morning asking if we wished to buy dressed lambs, saying that he was advised that we were without lambs. The price which he asked us for dressed lambs was a half cent per pound more than Canada Packers' price to the retail trade.
Fortunately, we were able to contact a feeder in the country who came to our help. We were able to purchase approximately half of our requirements from this feeder and will be forced to accept only half of our regular lamb trade, which as you can readily see, will seriously affect our dressed beef and veal trade.
This vicious practice has happened on five different occasions since the beginning of the year.
Until this week we have been successful in obtaining our full requirements of lambs either by bringing car loads in from Laeombe, Alberta and Lethbridge, Alberta, or purchasing small amounts from Ontario feeders, who, incidentally would rather sell to a small wholesaler than to the big packers.
These feed lot lambs, however, are rapidly diminishing and before long we shall be forced to go on the union stock yards to purchase our entire requirements. What then shall we do if the Canada Packers persist in this unethical practice?
In fairness to the Swift Canadian Company we would point out that these people are the essence of fairness.
On several occasions when we have run short of lambs, Swift's have sold us lambs which they already had bought and charged us market price.
We have absolutely no quarrel with the Swift Canadian Company.
This organization (Swift's) were subjected to the same treatment on Tuesday at the hands of Canada Packers Limited as we, on Monday.
Swift's at present are feeding a number of lambs behind their West Toronto plant, and are, therefore, not a big factor on the stock yards at present.
On Tuesday, however, they (Swift's) required 200 lambs to round out their requirements.
There were four car loads of western lambs in the market Tuesday and once again the Canada Packers openly declared that they must have all the lambs or none.
Another very serious angle of this Swift incident is that Swift's were willing to pay $9.35 per 100 pounds for lambs; the entire four car loads were sold to Canada Packers at $9.25 per 100 pounds.
We understand that Swift's are taking this up with the authorities at Ottawa, and are also advising the owner that they had bid $9.35 per 100 pounds for his lambs.
The Canada Packers Limited know full well, that on an even price basis, the small wholesaler, in most cases will be given the business,
but as their method of doing business is "defeat your opponent by fair means or foul" the small wholesaler is placed at a serious disadvantage.
WTe do not ask for special privileges (we don't need them) but we do demand and expect British fair play.
We feel sure in placing this matter before you, that corrective measures will immediately be taken.
Yours sincerely,
Alexander Mackenzie, Limited.
The point which is made in the minister's letter and which I desire to emphasize is that Swift's offered to pay S9.35, whereas the whole lot was sold for $9.25. If the market were a free market, the fact that Swift's bid $9.35 for 200 would have had a tendency to raise the price to the $9.35 price level. But Canada Packers came along and said that they would not buy any if the lot were broken up.
The same thing is done right along with hogs. A double-decked car of hogs, containing possibly 150 animals, will come on the market. In that carload will be selects, bacons, heavies, butchers, lights and possibly some stags, boars and so forth. But those are the five principal types that will be found. Here you have a carload, mixed. Canada Packers come along and say this; If you want to sell your hogs, we will take them all. But these wholesalers want the butcher type. They are willing to buy the butcher hogs in that lot. Montreal market is an excellent market for heavy hogs, Montreal will take the heavy hogs if they can get them. But Canada Packers say: Nothing doing-give us the whole carload or nothing. That is done right along.
Now let me give you the effect of that from the price standpoint. Under the regulations the price is fixed by the bacon grade. We will say the bacon grade is nine. The exact differential is not in my mind at the moment, but the minister will correct me if I am wrong. The bacon grade, we will say, is nine. The premium is one dollar a hog for selects. The penalty for butchers, the next grade, is one dollar a hog, I think, and then the penalty for lights and for heavies is another dollar, and another dollar, or it may be $1.50 below the bacon price. But the wholesaler wants the butcher type. He prefers the butcher type to the bacon hog or the select. It suits his business. He would be willing to pay the bacon price or possibly the select price in order to get the butcher type, but he cannot get it. If he competes with Canada Packers he must take the whole carload. The commission man is not allowed to divide .them.

I do not want to interrupt, but I assume my hon. friend is aware that what he is suggesting was tried out at Montreal three years ago, and that the very men he is now saying wish to have that done expressed the desire to change back to the old method. In other words, they said they did not desire to carry on in the way my hon. friend suggests.

But the reason for that is this: It is not done in Toronto or Winnipeg, and those are the markets that control live stock in Canada. Toronto is the market that controls live stock in Canada, and the practices in Toronto-why, Mr. Chairman!-I digress but I will come back in a moment-if a farmer in northern Saskatchewan, yes or in the dried-out area of British Columbia at Prince George, or in the back districts of Ontario, brings in two or three head of cattle to the local market he is paid what the Toronto price is at ten o'clock in the morning. He has no bargaining power. He must take that price or take his cattle home. The significance of this thing is not appreciated, it seems to me, and yet it is fatal, in my opinion, to the whole live stock market of Canada.
I come back to the hog. Montreal will buy heavies. In Toronto there is a good market for the butcher type. These wholesalers would buy the butcher type. The same thing applies in the outlying districts. But by this stranglehold which Canada Packers have over the commission houses whom they will blacklist if they do not dance to their piping, these practices go on; they are going on to-day, and have gone on right along. The thing should be stopped, Mr. Chairman, and I say this to the minister in all due deference. I know it is not nice to get into difficulties with these large packing concerns, but I say there is a principle upon which these things can be done, and it is the duty of government to see that these principles are applied.
I hesitate to go into the story of the marketing of hogs, but I intended to do it and perhaps I might as well do it now. I have said it before and I want to emphasize it because until this situation is corrected the farmers of this country, the five millions of people living on Canadian farms, are not going to get a square deal. They are not getting it to-day, and they will not get it until these things are corrected.
It may be said that the matter of the price of hogs is not going to ruin the farming industry of Canada. But in the last ten years the live stock sales in this country have been

almost equal, I venture to say to the grain sales. They are at least one of the biggest factors in the life of the farmer, and if the farmer cannot get a fair price for his cattle and his hogs he is simply heading for bankruptcy, as farmers have been doing by the tens of thousands.
What is the method of fixing the price of the Canadian hog to-day? I have told this story before. There is a committee in England consisting of the English buyers-not Canadian representatives in England, but British buyers for British firms that are purchasing our goods. That committee sits once a week, I think on Wednesday, and announces the price which goes into effect on Thursday for the following week. That price of Canadian bacon on the British market is telegraphed back here to Canada Packers-I say Canada Packers advisedly because they get the whole business-and Canada Packers fix the price of hogs in Canada on the basis of the price of bacon in England. Now in the first place I challenge the soundness, shall I say, of that method of fixing the price, for this reason. In the last ten years we have not exported more than ten per cent of our hogs. In the last year the export has gone up to eighteen per cent, or some such figure, but in the last decade we have not exported more than ten per cent of our hogs. Now, the price of bacon fixes the price not only of that ten per cent but of the other ninety per cent for the whole of Canada. It may be argued that that is a fair barometer, but if that philosophy is sound, then let me put this: The Canadian farmer ought to be getting as high a price for his hogs in relation to the price of Canadian bacon on the British market as the Danish farmer or the Dutch farmer or the Irish farmer gets for his hogs in relation to the price of Danish, Dutch or Irish bacon on the British market. The question is, does he do so? Here are the facts, and it took me about two years to get them. I have not the schedules under my hand, but I have the facts very clearly in my mind.
The price of Dutch bacon runs somewhere near our own, with Irish and Danish bacon considerably higher, particularly Danish, from eight shillings often to fourteen shillings, a hundred. What I did find in my study was, that the differential, and mark you, it is argued in London that that is the proper basis on which to determine the price in Canada; let us accept that position-I did find that the spread as against Canadian bacon was double that as against Dutch, Danish or Irish. In other words, the packer in Canada was getting double the price-what is the term

the economists use? It has slipped me for the moment-the Canadian packer was getting double the spread on the price of hogs in relation to Canadian bacon on the British market that his competitors did. That is a fact that challenges both the method of marketing and the philosophy and the fairness of Canada Packers and other packers in relation to the price on the British market.
There is another thing. We have as a matter of fact, over the years, persisted in sending into the British market a grade of bacon lower than we are competent to send. That is, they mix into their export business lights, heavies and butchers, which are not the best type of bacon hog, instead of limiting their exports to the bacon hog or the selects. It is sometimes said by people who are somewhat careless that we cannot get enough selects or bacon hogs to supply the export trade. That is absolutely false. I have the facts. I do not know whether I can put my fingers on them readily, but I can say from memory, that last year there came on our markets many times the number of select and bacon hogs which would have taken care of the total export trade of Canada.
Is it many times the possible export trade?

Yes. I would say more than double. I am safe in saying more than double our quota, which we have not yet filled. It may be said, "Well, we are not going to denude the Canadian market." There is no need to denude the Canadian market, but one thing is certain. If you accept the philosophy that the price of bacon on the British market fixes the price of hogs in Canada, the only thing to do is to ship the best bacon you can to England and get the best price you can for it. Can we do that? Yes. Dumart and Schneider and the Owen Sound plant did it, and actually got a premium over Danish bacon. On one occasion they got one shilling and two shillings over Danish bacon. On the British market we can compete with Danish bacon, probably with not all our export but with a substantial portion of it, with a grade which would get the Danish price, and if we got the Danish price, which is eight shillings to fourteen shillings above the Canadian price, and if the price of Canadian hogs is based on the price on the British market, you can see what the farmer has lost. I made a calculation over a five year period, and I figured that the Canadian farmer had lost, because of this method of handling his business, $36,000,000 which he might have had in enhanced price had this practice not been in vogue.

I do not want to take the time to reply to all that has been said, but there are some things that might be answered. My information is that all the bacon of the select and bacon types which is available at plants for export is exported, and that is the complete export.

Well, I have the figures.
They are all in the government statistics. I have winnowed them out, but whether I can lay my hands on them at the moment I am not sure.

The reason for the
extra amount of lower grades is the fact that the higher grades are not available.

That is not the case.
If I had the time I could find the facts. I submit that there was more than twice as much bacon and select hogs on the market last year than was necessary for the processing of the bacon that was exported.

Just to get the full information, there may be double the number necessary to supply the trade; but when you make provision for bruises; for those that are softs; for those that are culled out for different reasons, and for those which do not go to plants that export bacon-when you make provision for all that, all that is left goes to the export market.

While the hon. member was a minister of the government.

While I was a minister. The Agriculture officers, as far as I recall, did not open their mouths. They turned to Mr. Todd and Mr. Sales Manager whose name I have forgotten. can keep down the price on ten per cent, by putting inferior hogs into the making of bacon for that market, you keep down the price on the ninety per cent.
I make this further statement. If Canada Packers put out the bacon they could put out on the standard of Dumart's or Schneider's or some of the other small packers, and raised the price of standard bacon in England, they would have to find another million dollars of working capital, and that is another reason why they do not want to raise the price here. I do not want to delay the committee unduly, but I make this statement in regard to this practice that I have disclosed with respect to these lambs: It is one indication of dozens of cases of which I know. These people disclose their name and everything about the matter; and if the practice in question, namely, of Canada Packers going on the live stock markets of Canada and telling the commission houses that they must sell all or none, is allowed to continue, then every day we allow it to continue the farmers of Canada are defrauded of those fairer returns which they are entitled to receive for their products. If one had time, one could go into the sale of cattle, one could discuss the trucking business and show how Canada Packers will provide facilities for the truckers, fill their gasoline tanks so that they may be able to bring farmers' produce to them. Canada Packers' plant. They do not go on the live stock market at all. The live stock markets of Canada at Winnipeg and Toronto particularly are a joke and a by-word, though they were established for the purpose of maintaining an element of free competition for the farmers' products, where the farmer could take his hogs and his cattle and expect to get the advantage of competitive buying and selling. But that element of competition is not there because of the overwhelming and pernicious influence of Canada Packers.

Of course, even if I had the time I would not take the trouble to try to defend Canada Packers or any other packing concern, but in the minute or two that is left before six o'clock I wish to make this statement. I do not regard the letter which was written to the hon. member for
Kootenay East as typical of a condition that exists in connection with the marketing of live stock in Canada whether at Toronto or Winnipeg or elsewhere. If the person who wrote the letter had intended to have the matter investigated at the earliest possible date and in the natural way in which anyone expects .to have a matter of that kind investigated, he would naturally have written to the Department of Agriculture. But he apparently wanted a speech of the type we have heard this afternoon with regard to it.

I rise to a point of order. The minister is not stating the case as it is disclosed in the correspondence, or as it was disclosed in the correspondence from myself to him, to which attention was directed on March 11.

The hon. member himself directed it to the department, and he did the proper thing in directing it there. But the person who wrote the letter in the first place could just as well have written it to the department and had the matter investigated directly. Of course, there is a reason which is made apparent in the correspondence itself. This man had been in the habit of buying all his lambs from drovers and others here and there outside the yards altogether; when he was short on a certain day he went and asked for a certain number from someone else who had purchased them in the yards, and all he is complaining about is the fact that this particular packing concern did not see fit to give him the 200 lambs which he required at a certain time at a certain price. One may be able to criticize Canada Packers or any other packing concern for not being as courteous to someone else in the trade as they might have been, but I do not see that you can go very much further in criticism in connection with that particular matter. In other words, I do not think it is a typical case upon which to base the kind of criticism to which we have just listened. There may be all sorts of reasons for that type of criticism; but from investigations I made myself in England, and from the investigation the committee which was over there last summer made, and which one of my hon. friends commented upon highly-it dealt with the same thing-an entirely different reason is given for the lower price of bacon in Great Britain. We must, of course, take the information we obtain from those whom we pay to get information for us, until such time as that information is proven wrong.

The minister is not referring to the report-
Validity of Alberta Statutes

I am referring to the report of the committee that went over last year. That report is just as authentic, and the information received is as reliable, as that received even by the price spreads committee. This information was gathered at the source.
The report was a travesty.

It was, of course, critical of some people; it was critical of some activities in the past. But because it was critical it does not follow that it was a travesty. After all, the bacon industry is one that has been very carefully investigated, very carefully checked by the department, and while we are not satisfied with all the actions of the packing concerns, I do not think anyone can base the type of criticism to which we have listened this afternoon merely upon the assumption that some price is set over in Britain for some particular reason.
